word.shortDefinition: Says who or what goes together, or how you travel.

intro.title: Small word, one strict rule
paragraphs: Mit means 'with', and you'll use it constantly: with friends, with milk, with the bus. The meaning is easy.
The challenge is the grammar. Mit always takes the dative, every time, no exceptions. Learn the dative endings with mit and you've learned them for a dozen other prepositions too.

etymology.title: Where it comes from
etymology.summary: Mit is an old Germanic word for 'with'. English used to have it too: it survives in 'midwife', literally the 'with-woman' who stays with the mother.

tables.title: mit + dative
tables.intro: After mit, every article and possessive takes its dative ending.
notes: In the dative plural the noun itself usually gets an extra -n: mit den Kindern.
Pronouns change too: mit mir, mit dir, mit ihm, mit ihr, mit uns, mit Ihnen.

keyTrap.title: The big trap: forgetting the dative
keyTrap.explanation: Learners often use the plain form after mit. It always needs the dative ending.

wrong.german: Ich gehe mit mein Bruder ins Kino.

correct.german: Ich gehe mit meinem Bruder ins Kino.
correct.literal: I go with my brother to the cinema.

correct.german: Ich gehe mit meiner Schwester ins Kino.
correct.literal: I go with my sister to the cinema.

commonMistakes.title: Travelling 'by'
commonMistakes.explanation: English says 'by train'. German says 'with the train', and it needs the article.

commonMistakes.title: On foot is different
commonMistakes.explanation: Walking isn't mit anything: zu Fuß.

commonMistakes.title: Coming along
commonMistakes.explanation: Mit is also a separable prefix. At the end of a question it means 'along'.

sampleSentences.german: Sie fährt jeden Tag mit dem Bus.
sampleSentences.english: She takes the bus every day.

sampleSentences.german: Ich wohne mit zwei Freunden zusammen.
Wir gehen ins Kino. Kommst du mit?
sampleSentences.english: We're going to the cinema. Are you coming?

quiz.explanation: Ich becomes mir in the dative.
Der Bus is masculine, so the dative is dem.

memoryHook: Mit is always with the dative, and the dative is always with mit: mit dem, mit der, mit dem, mit den.
